explain.say: George Stephenson built his early railways with rails four feet eight and a half inches apart, one thousand four hundred and thirty five millimetres. That accident of history is now the standard gauge on most of the world's railways. On the board, a railway track cut open from the rail down to the soil.

explain.say: A train wheel presses hard on a tiny patch of steel. A twenty five tonne axle puts about a hundred and twenty three kilonewtons on each wheel. Look at how it is spread: the rail shares it among several sleepers about six hundred millimetres apart, and the sleepers press on deep, sharp stone called ballast. Why sharp stone, not smooth pebbles?

explain.say: Sharp stones lock together and grip the sleepers, while letting rain drain straight through. Now gauge, the distance between the rails. Look at the sizes: India's broad gauge is one thousand six hundred and seventy six millimetres, wider than standard, while Cape and metre gauges are narrower. Where two gauges meet, trains cannot cross.

Modern rail is welded into lengths of many kilometres, so it cannot expand at joints. Instead it is squeezed or pulled. It is laid at a stress-free temperature, here thirty degrees. At sixty degrees in the sun, the stress is about seventy two megapascals of squeeze, over five hundred kilonewtons in a sixty kilogram rail. The ballast must hold it from buckling sideways.

explain.say: Finally, how do trains stay on? Look at the wheels: they are slightly coned, wider at the inside. If the wheelset drifts right, the right wheel rolls on a bigger radius and steers it back. Clever! Exam tip: list each layer with its job. Challenge: on a zero degree winter night, is the rail squeezed or pulled, and by how much?

faq.q: What are the parts of a railway track?
faq.a: From the top: the steel rails, fastenings and rail pads, sleepers of concrete or timber, a deep layer of crushed stone ballast, a sub-ballast blanket and the formation soil.
Ballast spreads the sleeper loads onto the formation, holds the sleepers in line against sideways and lengthways forces, drains water away and lets the track be re-levelled by tamping.
The distance between the inner faces of the two rails. Standard gauge is 1,435 millimetres; India's broad gauge is 1,676 millimetres; metre gauge is 1,000 millimetres.

faq.q: Why do welded rails not buckle in summer?
faq.a: Continuous welded rail is laid and stressed at a chosen neutral temperature, and heavy sleepers with full ballast shoulders resist sideways movement. The rail carries the thermal stress, about 2.4 megapascals per degree, instead of expanding.

faq.q: How do train wheels stay on the rails?
faq.a: The wheel treads are coned, so a wheelset that drifts sideways rolls on a larger radius on one side and steers itself back to the centre. Flanges are only a last line of defence.

facts: Standard gauge is 1,435 mm (4 ft 8½ in); Indian broad gauge is 1,676 mm.
Rail steel expands about 11.5 millionths of its length per degree Celsius, so a fully restrained rail gains about 2.4 MPa of stress per degree.
